I absolutely recommend this game wholeheartedly; it's been over a year since I've been this immersed and emotionally invested into a game.  The game makes a point, but it's never heavy-handed about it; I really appreciate that, since too many stories of this nature is ruined by the author's soapbox.  The short pool of characters, and the fact that you are digging into aspects of their lives, learning information that they wouldn't tell anyone else, results in a special level of investment in the world.

It's nice to see a game where your choices do actually matter; the story branches out depending on what you do.  And while it does follow the same parallels, and generally tie back into itself at the end, it's not in such a way that negates the choices you've made up until that point.  The link between your choices and the results is usually sensical, and generally tied to how diligent you are in the game as opposed to needing a guide or crystal ball.  Usually, anyways; there is one situation where doing an objectively better job leads to an objectively worse result and (to me) felt like it should have been avoidable if I had just done better, but nope.  It's a fly in the ointment, but it's not bad enough to spoil the obvious care that's gone into this game.

There are a couple more minor niggles here and there; for example, I wish the game made it more clear that the information above a submittable piece of information is exactly what gets added, as opposed to a summary.  Relatedly, make it clear that they act on the information given without outside context.  This being unclear at the beginning tripped me up a couple times.

It's amazing how internally consistent the game is; nothing happens out of the blue, and if you look back (or on a second playthrough), you can see the events in retrospect.  The in-game rules aren't broken, either.  It's actually rather impressive.

The only major downside I can think of to the game is the general lack of replay value.  The first time through, you'll probably take about five hours or so.  The second time would be to go back and see everything as it occurs with the benefit on knowing the truth, plus more achievements.  Another playthrough or two after that to mop up achievements, if you really want to.  The game has no way of restarting the current day, or from a previous day, and only has one save file that overwrites itself automatically after every choice you make, so most of your time in subsequent playthroughs will be watching conversations that can't be skipped or sped up.

On balance with the replay value, and the skill and care that went into the game, I'd definitely say it's worth the ten dollar price point.  As I said at the start, it's a game that's had me more enthralled than any game I've played in the last year.  If you like this sort of thing, definitely give it a shot.

Don't let the barebones presentation fool you - as soon as you start delving into the evidence you'll be drawn into a thrilling detective story and a thoughtful thematic debate between security and privacy. I was surprised at how engrossing it is, even with the story told entirely through text and images.

The characters are very well written and are the highlight of the game. At first they seem like simple archetypes, but as you glean more information about them they become three dimensional, even sympathetic. Moral dilemmas arise as you decide what information to report back to your supervisor - which can have drastic effects on how events play out.

Do yourself a favour and go in blind, and make sure you take in as much information as you can instead of just instantly dragging the datachunks into the database - the writing and worldbuilding is by far the best part.

Although probably considered a "short" game by most (I played through the entire thing in one sitting in about 4-5 hours), I thrououghly enjoyed this game! I was surprised with how well written it was, each character had a distinct personality that I felt I could connect with, making the subject matter all the more real.

It is not without its problems though. The biggest issue I noticed was in determining what pieces of data needed to be uploaded to advance the story. In the beginning they flat out tell you that you don't have to upload everything, however I often found myself encountering pieces of information I felt not pertinent to the subject matter or specifics of the investigation at the time, but without uploading theses, the story would not progress. I am not sure if this is me misunderstanding the mechanics, a flaw in the story scripting, or a comment on how invasive survailance really can be.

Although most characters were well written, I felt like a few too many were "bi-polar", totally changing personality and actions out of nowhere. Again, I'm not sure if this was how it was written from the start, or if I uploaded enough of the "right" snippets to trigger these outcomes.

Overall, very well written, although I'm not sure how much replay value it has. I'd give it a solid 8/10

You're a recently hired investigator on Orwell, a newly introduced mass surveillance system. There's a terrorist attack, and you're put to work to find the perpetrators - sounds innocent enough? Over the course of the game, more is revealed through connections between characters. Who is behind all this? What are the motivations of each character? What on Earth is Thought? Nothing escapes Orwell - text messages, calls, website, computers - yet there is so much that escapes us. The plot gets more convoluted: Orwell becomes personal. Relevations abound. To what extent are we willing to sacrifice privacy for security?
An engrossing, narrative-based game. Like Firewatch or Gone Home, but you're sitting in front a computer screen the entire game. And there are a bit more choices to be made.

Rating: 9/10

Orwell is a visual novel kind of game that gives you the tools to snoop into people's bank accounts, computers, private conversations and social media sites. You will have to decide which pieces of information are relevant and whether you will reveal your subject's most intimate secrets to the government surveillance program. You gradually build networks and figure out various connections.

I really like the style and feel of the game. It's easy to think that Orwell gives you the opportunity to play the bad guy who merely rats out people who try to change the world for better, but in the end it's hard to point fingers. Orwell is not black and white.

The ORWELL system is a governmental program to monitor the digital activity of its citizens (as the Dec 2016 UK Investigatory Powers Bill comes into force, I can't help but see the irony). As you progress through the game, and are drawn into the role of digital detective (selecting the information to go to the authorities), the impact of your decisions, on what information to reveal and what to dismiss (and when, and in what context), is shown to have a real effect on the fate of the plot and the cast. Will you endeavour to solve the mystery you are presented with using research and time, or abuse your power and pass judgement yourself? Who will you trust? By story's end, will thoughts be free, or will Big Brother be watching over all? Remeber citizen, you have nothing to fear...

Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.

Creepy and well-written, Orwell tells the tale of what happens when the state gets unfettered access to your communication data, whether that be from the telephone or the internet. It's very topical, but it should be added that the scope of the access you have makes the recent "Snooper's Charter" in the UK look like lightweight. Nevertheless, your ability to screw with people's lives really hits home, especially when the twist at the end is revealed and all the consequences of your actions - and how misinterpreted data can be overblown - is laid bare.


That said, the game stays rather neutral in its moralising. It's clear the developers are anti-surveillance, as those *for* it would find the moral ambiguity of this game inconvenient, but they are not trying to whack you over the head with ideology. If you decide to come to the conclusion that, despite being messy at times, surveillance is a necessary evil then this game allows you to come to that conclusion. But it's going to push the extremes of what all-encompassing surveillance can do before it lets you come to that conclusion.

And while the politics of this game are clearly unavoidable, Orwell is also a pretty neat detective story, if not very typical. Instead of being in the front line looking for evidence, your sleuthing is invisible, but otherwise it has all the hallmarks of a good whodunnit, including red herrings, characters with strong motivations, and a twist at the end.

I'm not sure what else to say, really. It's pretty good and I happily recommend it.

Orwell is, as you might guess from the title, a near-future dystopian terrorism thriller told through the lens of the titular national surveillance system of a fictional country called simply The Nation. You learn about the characters through their chat logs, social media and blog posts etcetera and slowly build up a picture of what is going on. But will it be the right picture, or will it lead to more bombings? Will the guilty parties get arrested or will law enforcement focus on the wrong targets? All this and more is up to you, as a faceless "investigator" assigned to the Orwell mass surveillance project.

It looks like it was originally released episodically but it works just as well playing it all the way through. But remember: the system only makes connections based on the data YOU upload to it. If you pick the wrong information, things can go sideways very badly.

I picked this game up in the Christmas 2016 sale and have enjoyed my first playthrough greatly, so I highly recommend it for anyone looking for a story and character driven thriller of this kind. Do be prepared for a lot of clicking, scrolling and dragging and dropping though.

Orwell is something just simply caught my eye, something that I thought looked interesting; not unlike going through a large bin filled with various games of various quality, and it was on sale even. Orwell sets you up with a very old question, "How much security, is too much security?" The game puts you in control of a system that is essenically the worlds largest surveillance system, and not a whole lot of rules of what you can and cannot do. 

The gameplay itself is simple: Find what you need, attach it to the right person. The game mostly holds your hand by highlighting more or less EVERYTHING you can use, and even has a "star" next to a page that still has information you missed. The real trick are the "conflicting" databanks: you can only choose one, and whichever one you choose will determine how the end of the chapter plays out (and certain achievements).

If anything Orwell reminds me of a much more "personal" Papers Please. You are a security person who must go through several people to find out if they are legit or not. Except instead of person after person, its file after file..... and on a much more private scale.

I infringed suspects' privacies for the safety of my people. Suspects tried to make me turn on my government. But little did they realize I have no sympathy for suspected terrorists. Big brother: 1; Terrorists: 0.

10/10 would play again and see what a weak-willed government agent would be tempted to do.
Choices matter, no joke.

Some people have called this game Orwellian (hell, it's in the name), and likened it to Nineteen Eighty-Four or Papers, Please. Personally, I'd argue its value is far greater than that; Nineteen Eighty-Four was written nearly 70 years ago and Arstotzka is an almost comically totalitarian state, but Orwell is set in what could very easily be any present-day democracy... and feels like it's set in one, too. In Orwell you are not working for glorious Arstotzka or in service to Big Brother, blithely stamping out potential traitors left, right and centre; you and all the other characters you interact with are genuinely trying to protect the people of The Nation from an evidently real terrorist threat. You spend the game trying to do good, trying to protect people, you and the supporting characters agonising over whether this data-gathering is really necessary...

...and then the game makes sure you realise what you've done. Superb.

[i]Don't read too much about it, just do yourself a favour and go in entirely blind about the [b]story.[/b][/i]

[h1]Here's the things you need to know[/h1]

[*] This isn't like any game you've played before, the gameplay is weird and more or less takes place in a 'super powerful' browser.
[*] You are not a hacker
[*] You will liken it to a telltale game, yet it is much more subtle in how it plays.
[*] let it move you
[*] [b]don't just read the data chunks[/b] be prepared to read everything, you'll learn more about the story that way.
[*] It plays like a book
[*] Forgive my excitement and hyping, but it's for good reason.

That's all you [b]"need"[/b] to know.
if you're interested, download the demo and try it out.


[b]Also: Cool developers for allowing the game to have a demo which is a fully playable segment of the actual game, and not a controlled showcase.[/b]
Brilliant game! The story so far has been amazing. I don't often write reviews for games but this is incredibly on point.

Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.

I will start off by saying, I am not traditionally a text-based gamer. Orwell is a game that basically adapts the "Big Brother" aspect from the book 1984 by George Orwell (see where the game title came from?)

In short, you invade people's privacy, like analyze through their blog and social media, read their chats and emails, and even listen to their calls, to find who is actually behind the bombings on Bonton, a city of The Nation.

This game will put your decision-making to the test, because your choice impacts the game in every way, like blocking a credit card from buying a wine or decide whether this particular person is a terrorist or not. You can make them innocent or a criminal in just a single click.

What I enjoy best is the part when I'm in a dilemma on which one should I choose from conflicting data of a person. Should you turn them in because they "injured a police officer in rage", or should you make them innocent because they "injured a police officer to protect someone"? It's up to your brain to figure out which.

10/10 would be Big Brother again.

I did feel that the game could have 'allowed for failure' more - most of the time the decisions are binary and easy to predict. Putting more interesting choices about what data we can upload and the effects it would have improved it, I feel.

The game does do something like this at one point - minor spoiler – [spoiler] the amount of datachunks you can upload becomes limited. That means you spend more time agonising over what kind of data you should or shouldn’t upload. Which is great! You can only explore certain paths. It felt way too on rails before this point.[/spoiler]

Putting other constraints like time, far more bad data (maybe having to input data yourself rather than just highlighting and dragging it?) – in essence, raising the interactivity could drastically improve it. What spoils it for me is realising that I was never going to massively fail, I could just scroll through each highlighted source and pick everything out. Her Story had none of the same problems, you were free to explore each narrative in any order you wanted.

Anyway – enjoyed it a lot. Felt more could be done with the format, but a great exploration of how detective narratives can be done, and loved the themes (I felt myself uploading less info to Orwell as I grew more uncomfortable with how invasive it was getting). I look forward to a detective game or something that picks up on the same style.

[h1] DISCLAIMER: This is a full review, and NOT a first impressions review like all my other reviews, if you want a better full review, then please read better reviews then mine [/h1]

[quote] PLEASE NOTE: This review is being cast as a full review and not a first impressions review because the main bulk of the game is finished, although Orwell does have a story mode, it has different endings and choices, hence, this review is being cast as full because the main bulk of the game is complete, so please, think before you comment! Enjoy :) [/quote]

Orwell is a game developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Surpise Attack Games. Orwell is a compelling detective story that questions your morals, tugs your heart strings, and leaves you stunned. It has an intriguing plot that keeps you telling yourself "just one more episode..."

It does have some interesting characters who are easy to become attached to but not for long due to its short story and the game is intellectually satisfying. The game expects to absorb the world it has built and use deductive reasoning to back up your decisions and lines of investigation, basically meaning, it doesn't treat you like an idiot

However, Orwell is a fairly short game, finishing just one story with one ending in 2-3 hours is pretty damn short and currently there are no revising chapters and changing decisions. You have to create a new save from the beginning to pick different choices, however the developers have stated that they will change this in the near future with a patch

Orwell plays similar to a detective visual novel. If you are looking for flashy cutscenes and first/third person character control, then this is not the game for you. You are an intelligence agent working at your computer, and that is how you will experience this world. In my opinion, you do not need fancy graphics to appreciate the depth of this amazing story!

Orwell pays homage to one of the greatest writers of all time; George Orwell himself who has created some classic literary works such as Animal Farm and 1984 which this is inspired from!

[h1] RECOMMENDED :) [/h1]
